live_variations.description: Live arrangements frequently strip back the studio version's charango and synth-bass loop. Acoustic sessions (like their 'In The Open' or 'Beach House' series) often feature raw instrumentation, acoustic guitar, or even string quartets.

Sameer Gadhia employs dynamic variation, utilizing breathy, intimate vocal tones in the verses and adding subtle vocal runs, elongated notes, and emotional ad-libs during the latter sections of the song.
The band retains the standard 85 BPM tempo but plays around the 'pocket' of the syncopated groove live, allowing it to feel more fluid and improvisational compared to the rigid studio track.

live_variations.description: Serves as a massive audience participation track. Sameer Gadhia frequently points the microphone to the crowd, prompting them to sing key chorus lines ('If I could find a way...') or the post-chorus vocal hooks.
The song is occasionally performed at a slightly relaxed, heavier tempo (~125-127 BPM compared to 129 BPM canonical) to emphasize the emotional weight and anthemic nature of the chorus.
Gadhia adds dramatic vocal flourishes and extended, soaring high notes during the bridge and final chorus, leaning into the song's themes of frustration and escapism.

live_variations.description: Sameer Gadhia pushes his vocals to a raw, gritty limit live. He adds vocal grit, rhythmic staccato delivery, and improvisational pitch changes on the key phrases ('My body tells me no!').

Typically performed as a high-energy set closer or encore piece. The band encourages the audience to jump in unison and sing along with the main hooks. The bridge's repetition of 'It's my road / It's my war' is structured as a powerful call-and-response.

The song is kept close to its original driving rock tempo (~130 BPM), but the band often extends the outro or introduces subtle instrumental pauses before the explosive final chorus to maximize the crowd's energy.

The band maintains the upbeat tempo (~78 BPM in a half-time feel/156 BPM equivalent) but leans heavily into live synthesizer layers and energetic guitar interplay to create a massive wall of sound. In acoustic sets, they strip this down to a soft piano and acoustic guitar ballad.

live_variations.description: Frontman Nathan Willett alternates between a soulful lower register in the verses and a strained, high-pitched shout during the chorus. He often punctuates the phrase 'too, too, too many times' with rhythmic, staccato vocal delivery or lets the crowd take over the line.

Known for a much looser, bluesier feel live. The band frequently engages in erratic, free-jazz style piano flourishes, discordance, and extended instrumental jams that expand beyond the tightly wound studio arrangement.

While keeping to the standard driving bass line, the band plays with the song's tension, stretching out the transition zones or slightly accelerating during the peak choruses before dropping back into the dry groove.

live_variations.description: The song features a highly interactive section during the chorus chant 'Put out the fire, boys / Don't stop, don't stop / Put out the fire on us'. Nathan Willett frequently steps away from the mic and coordinates a call-and-response sing-along with the audience.
Live, the piano is played as a heavy percussive instrument. The percussion section is often amplified with additional drums, maracas, or tambourines, adding to the song's bluesy, chaotic climax.
The band plays with the dynamic contrast, stripping down the verses to just Willett's vocals and basic piano before building up to a loud, floor-stomping pace during the 'Put out the fire' choruses.

live_variations.description: In live settings, the band frequently extends the intro with a prominent, driving bass and drum groove, building anticipation before Nathan Willett enters with the first verse.

As one of their biggest modern hits, the chorus 'How am I the lucky one? / I do not deserve to wait around forever...' is turned into a major sing-along, where Willett often lets the crowd take over the vocal melody entirely.

The outro section is often extended live, with Willett delivering soulful, improvised vocal ad-libs, repeating the key lines with increasing emotional intensity over a building wall of sound from the band.

live_variations.description: Often opens with Nathan Willett performing a solo piano intro before the band joins. This sparse beginning heightens the narrative storytelling quality of the verses.

A landmark of their live sets. The song is frequently stretched beyond studio length with an improvised, blues-inflected instrumental jam. Willett occasionally plays maracas while the rhythm section drives the groove.
Spotlighted on the Robbers & Cowards 20th anniversary set, this song receives extended treatment as a centerpiece. Crowd sing-along of the chorus is very common with longtime fans.

The 'come up for air' refrain is ideally structured for audience participation. Willett frequently sings the lead line and points the mic to the crowd to answer, especially in the extended bridge/outro.

The chorus is short, punchy, and highly singable. Crowds often come in strong on 'you'll always be that sunburn on me.'
